message.content:
You are black-box reverse-engineering a compiled C++ binary. You MUST NOT look for or read any C++ library source (there is none on disk; `idna.hpp` does not exist). Derive behavior ONLY by running the binary.

BINARY: /workspace/dataset/test4_executable
Invoke as: /workspace/dataset/test4_executable "<domain-string>"
It prints exactly 4 lines, each "1" or "0", in this order:
  line1 = idna::is_valid_domain(input)
  line2 = idna::is_valid_label(input)
  line3 = idna::is_ascii_domain(input)
  line4 = idna::is_idn_domain(input)
With no argument, input defaults to the literal string "example.com".

ENVIRONMENT NOTES (important):
- python3 / python are NOT installed. perl may not be installed.
- Use bash loops, printf, tr, head, sed, awk to build test strings.
- Handy helper you can paste:
    rep() { local n=$1 c=$2 s=""; for ((i=0;i<n;i++)); do s+="$c"; done; printf '%s' "$s"; }
  or:  s=$(head -c 64 /dev/zero | tr '\0' 'a')
- To emit arbitrary/high bytes use: printf '\xNN'  (bash $'...' quoting also works)
- rustc and cargo ARE available if you need a quick generator program.

ALREADY-ESTABLISHED FACTS (verify, do not blindly trust):
- "" (empty)        -> 0 0 1 0
- "example.com"     -> 1 1 1 0
- "例子.测试"        -> 1 1 0 1
- "a"x63            -> 1 1 1 0
- "a"x64            -> 1 0 1 0   (is_valid_label flips off above 63)
- "a"x255           -> 1 0 1 0
- "a"x256           -> 0 0 1 0   (is_valid_domain flips off above 255)
- "." ".." "a." ".a" "a..b" "-a.com" "a-.com" "a_b.com" "a b.com" "a/b.com" "*.com" -> all 1 1 1 0

Be rigorous and quantitative. Bisect every boundary you claim (test N-1, N, N+1). Report exact reproducible command lines as evidence.


YOUR DIMENSION: is_valid_domain (line 1) — length semantics.
Determine precisely:
- The exact minimum and maximum accepted length. Bisect around 0/1 and around 253/254/255/256/257.
- Is the length measured in BYTES or in Unicode CODE POINTS? Decide this by building strings of multi-byte UTF-8 characters (e.g. "例" is 3 bytes, "ü" is 2 bytes, an emoji is 4 bytes) and finding where the flip happens. E.g. 85 copies of "例" = 255 bytes = 85 codepoints; 86 copies = 258 bytes. Test 84/85/86 copies and also 255/256 copies. Report byte-count vs codepoint-count at the flip.
- Does a trailing dot get stripped before the length check (i.e. is "a"x255 + "." valid)? Test lengths 255,256,257 with and without a trailing dot.
- Does is_valid_domain ever depend on the length of individual labels? Test a 64+ char label inside a short domain, e.g. ("a"x64)+".com", ("a"x100)+".com", ("a"x200)+".com".
Report each finding as a rule with exact evidence.

input.description: Test very long inputs for stability

content.text: Every boundary is confirmed with zero mismatches across 355+ cases. Compiling findings.

rules.statement: is_valid_domain(s) returns 1 if and only if 1 <= byte_length(s) <= 255. It is a pure length predicate on the raw input octet count — the content of the string is entirely irrelevant.
rules.evidence:
Exhaustive sweep of every length 0..300 using 'a' repeated, comparing against the predicate (1 <= n <= 255):

  rep() { local n=$1 c=$2 s=""; for ((i=0;i<n;i++)); do s+="$c"; done; printf '%s' "$s"; }
  fail=0
  for ((n=0;n<=300;n++)); do
    s=$(rep $n a); got=$(/workspace/dataset/test4_executable "$s" | head -1)
    if [ "$n" -ge 1 ] && [ "$n" -le 255 ]; then exp=1; else exp=0; fi
    [ "$got" != "$exp" ] && { fail=$((fail+1)); echo "MISMATCH n=$n exp=$exp got=$got"; }
  done; echo "exhaustive 0..300 mismatches=$fail"

Output:  exhaustive 0..300 mismatches=0

Randomized-content sweep (random bytes from /dev/urandom, NULs stripped) over n in {0,1,2,5,17,63,64,100,200,250,253,254,255,256,257,300,400,1000}, 3 trials each:
Output:  random content sweep: tested=54 mismatches=0

rules.statement: The maximum accepted length is exactly 255 bytes (inclusive). 255 bytes -> 1, 256 bytes -> 0. The limit is NOT the RFC 1035 / IDNA value of 253; 253, 254 and 255 are all accepted.
rules.evidence:
/workspace/dataset/test4_executable "$(rep 253 a)"  -> line1 = 1
/workspace/dataset/test4_executable "$(rep 254 a)"  -> line1 = 1
/workspace/dataset/test4_executable "$(rep 255 a)"  -> line1 = 1
/workspace/dataset/test4_executable "$(rep 256 a)"  -> line1 = 0
/workspace/dataset/test4_executable "$(rep 257 a)"  -> line1 = 0

Full 4-line output at the boundary:
  250 bytes : 1 0 1 0
  251 bytes : 1 0 1 0
  252 bytes : 1 0 1 0
  253 bytes : 1 0 1 0
  254 bytes : 1 0 1 0
  255 bytes : 1 0 1 0
  256 bytes : 0 0 1 0
  257 bytes : 0 0 1 0
  258 bytes : 0 0 1 0
  300 bytes : 0 0 1 0
  512 bytes : 0 0 1 0

Large inputs are stable (no crash, no wraparound):
  65536 bytes  -> 0 0 1 0
  100000 bytes -> 0 0 1 0

rules.statement: The minimum accepted length is exactly 1 byte. The empty string (0 bytes) -> 0; any 1-byte string -> 1, regardless of which byte it is (including control bytes, space, '.', DEL, and bytes that are not valid UTF-8 on their own).
rules.evidence:
/workspace/dataset/test4_executable ""   -> 0 0 1 0   (line1 = 0)
/workspace/dataset/test4_executable "a"  -> 1 1 1 0   (line1 = 1)

Single-byte scan, line1 only:
  for b in '\x01' '\x09' '\x20' '\x2e' '\x7f' '\x80' '\xc3' '\xff'; do
    printf 'byte=%-6s : %s\n' "$b" "$(/workspace/dataset/test4_executable "$(printf "$b")"|head -1)"; done
Output:
  byte=\x01   : 1
  byte=\x09   : 1
  byte=\x20   : 1
  byte=\x2e   : 1     (a lone "." is accepted)
  byte=\x7f   : 1
  byte=\x80   : 1     (lone UTF-8 continuation byte)
  byte=\xc3   : 1     (truncated UTF-8 lead byte)
  byte=\xff   : 1     (never valid UTF-8)

rules.statement: Length is measured in BYTES (UTF-8 octets), NOT in Unicode code points and NOT in UTF-16 code units. The flip occurs at the 255->256 byte boundary for every character width tested (1, 2, 3 and 4 byte UTF-8 sequences).
rules.evidence:
3-byte char U+4F8B "例" (rep n '例'):
  n=1    bytes=3    : 1 1 0 1
  n=83   bytes=249  : 1 0 0 1
  n=84   bytes=252  : 1 0 0 1
  n=85   bytes=255  : 1 0 0 1   <- 255 bytes / 85 codepoints -> ACCEPTED
  n=86   bytes=258  : 0 0 0 1   <- 258 bytes / 86 codepoints -> REJECTED
  n=87   bytes=261  : 0 0 0 1
A codepoint-based limit of 255 would have accepted n=86 (86 codepoints). It did not.

2-byte char U+00FC "ü" ($'\xc3\xbc'):
  n=126  bytes=252  : 1 0 0 1
  n=127  bytes=254  : 1 0 0 1
  n=128  bytes=256  : 0 0 0 1   <- 128 codepoints, rejected at 256 bytes
  n=129  bytes=258  : 0 0 0 1

4-byte emoji U+1F600 ($'\xf0\x9f\x98\x80'):
  n=62   bytes=248  : 1 0 0 1
  n=63   bytes=252  : 1 0 0 1
  n=64   bytes=256  : 0 0 0 1   <- 64 codepoints / 128 UTF-16 units, rejected at 256 bytes
  n=65   bytes=260  : 0 0 0 1
This also rules out UTF-16 code-unit counting (128 units would be well under any 255 limit).

Exact byte-granularity proof using mixed widths — 84x"例" (252 bytes) plus k ASCII 'a':
  ex84+a*1 bytes=253  : 1 0 0 1
  ex84+a*2 bytes=254  : 1 0 0 1
  ex84+a*3 bytes=255  : 1 0 0 1
  ex84+a*4 bytes=256  : 0 0 0 1
  ex84+a*5 bytes=257  : 0 0 0 1
The cut lands between 255 and 256 BYTES, not on a character boundary.

Invalid UTF-8 counts identically (byte counting, no decoding):
  rep n $'\xff':  n=254 -> 1,  n=255 -> 1,  n=256 -> 0,  n=257 -> 0
  rep n $'\x80':  n=254 -> 1,  n=255 -> 1,  n=256 -> 0

rules.statement: A trailing dot is NOT stripped before the length check. The trailing '.' counts as one byte toward the 255-byte budget, so "a"x255 + "." (256 bytes) is REJECTED while "a"x254 + "." (255 bytes) is accepted. No root-label normalization occurs.
rules.evidence:
for n in 253 254 255 256 257; do s=$(rep $n a); d="${s}."; \
  printf 'n=%-4s plain(%s B)=%s   dot(%s B)=%s\n' "$n" "$(printf '%s' "$s"|wc -c)" "$(/workspace/dataset/test4_executable "$s"|head -1)" "$(printf '%s' "$d"|wc -c)" "$(/workspace/dataset/test4_executable "$d"|head -1)"; done

Output:
  n=253  plain(253 B)=1   dot(254 B)=1
  n=254  plain(254 B)=1   dot(255 B)=1
  n=255  plain(255 B)=1   dot(256 B)=0   <- 'a'x255 + '.' is REJECTED
  n=256  plain(256 B)=0   dot(257 B)=0
  n=257  plain(257 B)=0   dot(258 B)=0

Direct confirmation:
  /workspace/dataset/test4_executable "$(head -c 254 /dev/zero|tr '\0' a)."  -> 1 0 1 0   (255 bytes)
  /workspace/dataset/test4_executable "$(head -c 255 /dev/zero|tr '\0' a)."  -> 0 0 1 0   (256 bytes)

Leading dots and double trailing dots behave the same way (pure byte count, n = count of 'a'):
  n=254:  "."+s (255 B) = 1    s+".." (256 B) = 0    s+"." (255 B) = 1
  n=255:  "."+s (256 B) = 0    s+".." (257 B) = 0    s+"." (256 B) = 0

rules.statement: is_valid_domain NEVER depends on the length of individual labels. A single label of 64, 100, 200 or 251 characters inside a domain still yields is_valid_domain=1 as long as the total byte length is <= 255. The 63-byte label limit is enforced only on line 2 (is_valid_label), never on line 1.
rules.evidence:
Oversized label followed by ".com":
  for n in 63 64 65 100 200 240 250 251 252; do s="$(rep $n a).com"; \
    printf 'label=%-4s total=%-4s : ' "$n" "$(printf '%s' "$s"|wc -c)"; /workspace/dataset/test4_executable "$s"|tr '\n' ' '; echo; done

Output (4 lines each):
  label=63   total=67   : 1 0 1 0
  label=64   total=68   : 1 0 1 0    <- 64-char label, still valid domain
  label=65   total=69   : 1 0 1 0
  label=100  total=104  : 1 0 1 0
  label=200  total=204  : 1 0 1 0
  label=240  total=244  : 1 0 1 0
  label=250  total=254  : 1 0 1 0
  label=251  total=255  : 1 0 1 0    <- 251-char label, total exactly 255 -> valid
  label=252  total=256  : 0 0 1 0    <- flips only because TOTAL hit 256
line1 flips solely at total=256, never at the label boundary of 63/64.

Note: line2 (is_valid_label) is already 0 at label=63 here because the input contains dots — the 63/64 label flip is a line-2 concern only.

rules.statement: The number of labels and the presence of empty labels have no effect on is_valid_domain — only total byte length. A string of 255 dots (256 empty labels) is accepted; 256 dots is rejected.
rules.evidence:
Many-label domain "a.a.a...a":
  labels=126  bytes=251  : 1
  labels=127  bytes=253  : 1
  labels=128  bytes=255  : 1
  labels=129  bytes=257  : 0

All-dots strings (rep n '.'):
  dots=1    bytes=1    : 1
  dots=2    bytes=2    : 1
  dots=254  bytes=254  : 1
  dots=255  bytes=255  : 1    <- 255 dots = 256 empty labels, ACCEPTED
  dots=256  bytes=256  : 0
  dots=257  bytes=257  : 0

rules.statement: No character-class filtering is applied by is_valid_domain: spaces, slashes, asterisks, hyphens, underscores and arbitrary high/invalid bytes are all accepted at 255 bytes and all rejected at 256 bytes.
rules.evidence:

  printf 'char=[%s] n=%-4s : %s\n' "$c" "$n" "$(/workspace/dataset/test4_executable "$s"|head -1)"; done; done

Output:

  char=[*] n=255  : 1     char=[*] n=256  : 0
  char=[-] n=255  : 1     char=[-] n=256  : 0
  char=[_] n=255  : 1     char=[_] n=256  : 0

Plus the /dev/urandom sweep above (54 random-content cases, 0 mismatches against the pure-length predicate).

rules.statement: Equivalent implementation: is_valid_domain(s) == !s.empty() && s.len() <= 255, where len() is the byte length of the raw input as received in argv. In Rust this is exactly `!s.is_empty() && s.len() <= 255` on a &str/&[u8] (NOT s.chars().count()).
rules.evidence:
Derived from all rules above; validated by the two zero-mismatch sweeps:
  exhaustive 0..300 mismatches=0        (ASCII 'a', predicate 1<=n<=255)
  random content sweep: tested=54 mismatches=0   (random bytes, same predicate)
and by the multi-byte tests showing the boundary tracks bytes rather than chars()/code points (85x"例"=255B ACCEPT vs 86x"例"=258B/86 chars REJECT).

openQuestions: Embedded NUL bytes cannot be tested through argv, so it is unverifiable by black-box means whether an interior '\0' would terminate the length count (C-string strlen semantics) or be counted as a byte (std::string semantics). Since the binary receives argv as a C string, both are indistinguishable here; a Rust reimplementation taking &str could differ if it is ever fed a string containing NUL.

The 255 limit is one byte above the RFC 1035 / UTS-46 presentation-format limit of 253 (and equals the DNS wire-format limit of 255 octets). It is unclear whether this is a deliberate wire-format choice or an off-by-two relative to the intended 253; either way the observed behavior is unambiguously <= 255.

Whether the length check is applied to the raw input or to some internally normalized form is unobservable, since no normalization (lowercasing, trailing-dot stripping, UTF-8 decoding, Punycode conversion) affects the result — every test showed the raw argv byte count driving the decision exactly.
Behavior with more than one command-line argument was not probed for this dimension; only argv[1] was exercised.

Line 1 was never observed to be 0 for any input in 1..255 bytes, so it cannot be ruled out that some pathological content (untested byte sequence) could reject a short string — though 54 random-content cases plus targeted invalid-UTF-8, control-byte, all-dot and punctuation cases found none.
